FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.93  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.86  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` can be called before any allocation exists and still permanently updates failure/convergence/fingerprint state from unallocated work.** The method accepts arbitrary `responses`, `findings`, and `tasks`, but never checks that an allocation was previously computed for this round, nor that the supplied evidence corresponds to any dispatched assignment. As a result, the manager can ingest synthetic or stray responses, emit recovery actions, advance the FSM, and adapt fingerprints without any actual scheduled work. This is deeper than “allocation is stored as `None`”: the orchestration boundary lacks a dispatch-to-observation invariant, so the system cannot distinguish real round evidence from arbitrary caller input.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.90  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.84  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` never validates that each response’s `round_idx` equals the manager’s current round, so stale/future responses can mutate the wrong round’s state.** The method keys all internal updates by `self.fsm.current_round`, but `FailureHandler.detect_failure()` and emitted events use `response.round_idx` directly. A caller can submit a response from round 7 while the manager is processing round 2; failure history, event logs, and `RoundResult.responses` will then contain internally inconsistent timestamps, while convergence and diminishing-returns state are updated under round 2. This is a distinct temporal-integrity flaw from findings about `Finding.round_idx` mismatch.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.88  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.82  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` never validates that the `responses` dictionary key matches `ModelResponse.model_id`, allowing identity spoofing inside failure handling.** The loop iterates `for model_id, response in responses.items()`, but then passes only `response` into `detect_failure()` and only later uses the outer `model_id` for `get_recovery()` and `record_failure()`. If the key is `"m1"` but `response.model_id` is `"m2"`, event emission and performance history are recorded under `"m2"` while recovery and role-failure history are applied to `"m1"`. This creates split-brain state across subsystems from a single malformed input.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.86  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION: 0.80  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager` has no notion of “expected responders for this round,” so silent non-response by an assigned model is fundamentally unobservable at the manager boundary.** Failure detection is purely response-driven: only models present in `responses` are examined. Without persisted allocation or expected-response roster, the system cannot infer that a missing response should count as `EMPTY`/`TIMEOUT`/transport failure. This is more structural than prior “missing responses are omitted” observations: the current API makes correct non-response detection impossible because the necessary expectation set is never represented in manager state.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.84  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.78  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` accepts findings from models that do not appear in `responses`, so evidence provenance is not enforced.** `findings` are fed directly into convergence detection and fingerprint updates regardless of whether the purported source model submitted a successful response this round. A malicious or buggy caller can therefore attribute findings to a non-responding or failed model and still have them counted toward convergence, novelty, and live capability adaptation. This is a separate provenance defect from generic unknown-model acceptance: even known active models can be credited with unsupported findings.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.82  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.77  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **A single response can be evaluated multiple times with cumulative side effects because `FailureHandler.detect_failure()` is not idempotent.** On every call, the UNDERPERFORM path appends to `_perf_history`; repeated evaluation of the same `ModelResponse` therefore changes future classifications. Since `DynamicManager.process_round()` does not guard against duplicate processing and stores caller-owned response objects by reference, retries/replays of the same logical round can escalate underperformance history and recovery policy without any new evidence. The missed issue is the absence of a response identity or de-duplication mechanism at the failure-handler boundary.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.80  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION: 0.74  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`FailureHandler.detect_failure()` treats `EMPTY` as higher priority than `TIMEOUT`, so a timed-out blank response is classified as `EMPTY` and can follow the wrong recovery path.** Because the checks are ordered `EMPTY -> TIMEOUT -> MALFORMED -> ...`, any transport failure represented as an empty payload with long response time is irreversibly collapsed into `EMPTY`. That matters because the recovery table distinguishes TIMEOUT (`RETRY_EXTENDED` / exclusion path) from EMPTY (`RETRY` / exclusion path), and timeout-specific observability is lost. This priority interaction was not explicitly identified in prior findings.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F008  
SEVERITY: 0.78  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.73  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`FailureHandler.detect_failure()` can silently treat a semantically impossible response as healthy because there is no validation on `finding_count` and `mean_abstraction` before computing performance.** Negative `finding_count`, negative `mean_abstraction`, or values above 1.0 are accepted and fed into `_performance_metric()`. Depending on sign and magnitude, these can suppress underperformance detection, create extreme ratios, or poison `_perf_history`. This is more specific than general “dataclasses accept bad numbers”: the failure policy directly consumes those values as decision inputs without sanitization.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F009  
SEVERITY: 0.76  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION: 0.76  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` can emit externally visible monitoring events before it knows whether the callback path will succeed, and before internal state mutation is complete, leaving observers with a causally inconsistent trace on exception.** `ManagerEventStream.emit()` records and forwards events synchronously. `process_round()` emits `ROUND_COMPLETE`, then later convergence/stop events, interleaved with mutations to failure history, FSM state, and fingerprint state. If a callback raises mid-sequence, some events are already durably recorded while the manager has only partially mutated state. Prior findings noted callback fragility; the missed cross-cutting issue is that the orchestration method has no transaction boundary around event publication versus state mutation.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F010  
SEVERITY: 0.74  
FLAW_CLASS: 1  
ABSTRACTION: 0.71  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`RoundProgressionFSM.select_event()` can return `COMPLETE` for `BLIND` or `SYNTH` without checking whether those phases are semantically satisfiable under the current configuration, so the FSM can advance through structurally invalid protocol shapes.** In particular, `max_rounds=1` still allows `BLIND -> SYNTH -> ROUND_1` via `COMPLETE` even though `max_round_idx=0`. Prior findings discussed validator breakage around this configuration; the deeper missed flaw is that the runtime FSM itself admits impossible phase transitions instead of rejecting the configuration or terminalizing directly.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F011  
SEVERITY: 0.72  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.69  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.get_allocation()` does not validate that task identifiers are unique before building an `Allocation`, so later allocation queries can become ambiguous even when the solver itself “succeeds.”** Duplicate `task_id`s collapse in `Allocation.model_load()`’s task map and make `get_assigned_models()` address only the first matching row. A caller can therefore receive an apparently valid allocation that cannot be interpreted consistently afterward. This is distinct from the already-verified duplicate-task issue in `LoadBalancer.__init__`: the manager never defends its public boundary against such invalid task sets.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F012  
SEVERITY: 0.70  
FLAW_CLASS: 4  
ABSTRACTION: 0.72  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.check_dispatch_feasibility()` is not coupled to the model’s active status or current run state, so it can endorse dispatch planning for models that the manager should no longer use.** The method accepts any `ModelSpec`, constructs a one-model `LoadBalancer`, and evaluates only token feasibility. It does not check `fsm.is_terminal`, active membership, or whether the model belongs to this manager instance. This is broader than prior findings about excluded models: the public planning API itself operates outside the manager’s lifecycle and authority constraints.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F013  
SEVERITY: 0.68  
FLAW_CLASS: 2  
ABSTRACTION: 0.67  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.__init__()` does not enforce that initial model IDs are non-empty, unique, and stable identifiers before wiring them into every subsystem.** Many internal maps are keyed by raw `model_id` strings; empty-string IDs or whitespace-only IDs would not collide at Python level but would collapse observability (`events_by_model`, logs, role_map readability, sentinel confusion with `"system"` patterns) and make debugging impossible. Duplicate IDs were separately observed elsewhere, but the broader identifier hygiene failure at construction remains unguarded.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F014  
SEVERITY: 0.66  
FLAW_CLASS: 6  
ABSTRACTION: 0.64  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`DynamicManager.process_round()` mixes pre-transition and post-transition semantics into a single `RoundResult` without recording the triggering event, making the result insufficient to reconstruct control flow.** `round_idx` refers to the processed phase before transition, `state` stores the post-transition state, and neither the selected `Event` nor the termination reason is captured in the result. Consumers therefore cannot reliably tell whether a result ended due to completion, convergence, diminishing returns, or failure without separately querying mutable manager state. This is a deeper API-design gap than simple state/round mismatch.

FINDING_ID: ROUND11_F015  
SEVERITY: 0.64  
FLAW_CLASS: 5  
ABSTRACTION: 0.61  
VERIFIED: FALSE  
DESCRIPTION: **`LoadBalancer._objective()` is not monotone with respect to infeasible overload on non-positive-capacity models: assigning work to a model with `L <= 0` can leave both bottleneck and variance artificially low.** Fractions are computed with `np.where(limits > 0, loads / limits, 0.0)`, so any overloaded zero-capacity model contributes `0.0` load fraction to both penalties. The allocation can therefore look cheaper and more balanced precisely when it is maximally impossible. Prior findings noted specific cases; the deeper missed point is that the objective function itself rewards certain infeasible allocations, not just fails to penalize them.

These are my new findings; I did not repeat the already-listed issues.
